cards.title: Samhain: the Celtic night behind Halloween
cards.body:
Long before costumes and candy, Gaelic peoples in Ireland and Scotland marked Samhain, a festival around October 31 and November 1 that closed the harvest and opened the dark half of the year. It was believed to be a time when the boundary between this world and the otherworld thinned, so spirits and fairies could cross over.

Communities lit bonfires, and in later centuries people went guising: dressing in disguise and going door to door, sometimes performing in exchange for food. Meanwhile, the church had set November 1 as All Saints', or All Hallows', Day, making October 31 All Hallows' Eve, later shortened to Halloween.

Irish and Scottish immigrants brought these customs to North America in the 1800s, where they blended with local traditions into the holiday we know. Trick-or-treating became widespread in the twentieth century.
cards.example: The name itself records the history: Hallowe'en is a contraction of All Hallows' Even, with hallow meaning saint. When kids knock on doors tonight, they're echoing a practice Scottish and Irish children called guising.
cards.takeaway: Halloween is a Celtic seasonal festival wearing a Christian name.

cards.title: Enterprise value: the price of the whole business
cards.body:
Market capitalization tells you what the equity costs, but if you bought an entire company you'd also inherit its debt and pocket its cash. Enterprise value (EV) captures that full takeover price: market cap plus debt, preferred shares and minority interests, minus cash and equivalents.

This matters because two companies with the same market cap can be wildly different bargains. One carrying heavy debt is effectively more expensive; one sitting on a pile of cash is cheaper than it looks.

EV pairs with measures that belong to all capital providers, like revenue, EBITDA or operating income, because those profits are earned before lenders are paid. Equity value pairs with measures that belong only to shareholders, like net income. Mixing them, such as dividing EV by net income, is a classic interview mistake.
cards.example: Companies A and B both have $10B market caps. A has $4B of debt and $1B of cash, so EV = $13B. B has no debt and $3B of cash, so EV = $7B. If both earn $1B of EBITDA, A trades at 13x EV/EBITDA and B at 7x, despite identical market caps.
cards.takeaway: EV is what you'd pay for the whole company: equity plus debt, minus cash.

cards.title: Point Nemo: the loneliest spot in the ocean
cards.body:
Somewhere in the South Pacific lies the point in the ocean farthest from any land. It's called Point Nemo, after Jules Verne's submarine captain, and it was pinpointed in 1992 by survey engineer Hrvoje Lukatela using computer modelling.

The nearest land, a trio of tiny islands, is roughly 2,700 kilometres away in each direction. The area is also remarkably empty of life: it sits inside a vast ocean gyre where the water carries few nutrients, so little grows near the surface.

Its remoteness makes it useful. Space agencies steer old satellites and spacecraft to crash into the sea around it, turning it into a spacecraft graveyard; Russia's Mir space station came down in this region in 2001. And because the International Space Station orbits roughly 400 kilometres up, astronauts passing overhead can be the closest humans to anyone at Point Nemo.
cards.example: Open a map and zoom out over the South Pacific between New Zealand and Chile. The nearest land to Point Nemo is Ducie Island in the Pitcairn group, Motu Nui near Easter Island, and Maher Island off Antarctica.
cards.takeaway: Point Nemo is so remote that the nearest people are often in orbit.

cards.title: Fleetwood Mac: Rumours
cards.body:
Few albums were made under stranger conditions. In 1976, as Fleetwood Mac recorded Rumours, Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks were breaking up, John and Christine McVie were divorcing, and Mick Fleetwood's marriage was falling apart. The band wrote songs about each other and then had to sing them together.

The result, released in 1977, is a polished soft-rock record full of tension: bright harmonies on top, heartbreak underneath. It became one of the best-selling albums of all time.

Listen for how each songwriter has a distinct voice. Buckingham's songs are sharp and nervy, Nicks's are mystical, and Christine McVie's are warm and hopeful. Start with Dreams, then Go Your Own Way, then The Chain, the only song credited to all five members, stitched together from separate pieces.
cards.example: Put on The Chain and wait for John McVie's bass line near the three-minute mark, when everything drops out and the song builds into its famous final section. Then play Dreams and notice how little the band actually plays behind Nicks's voice.
cards.takeaway: Rumours turned a band's breakups into one of rock's most loved albums.

cards.title: OK began as a newspaper joke in 1839
cards.body:
OK may be the most widely used word on the planet, and it started as a gag. In the late 1830s, Boston newspaper writers had a fad for comic abbreviations of deliberately misspelled phrases. On March 23, 1839, the Boston Morning Post printed o.k. for oll korrect, a jokey spelling of all correct.

Most of these jokes died quickly. OK survived thanks to politics. In the 1840 presidential election, supporters of Martin Van Buren, nicknamed Old Kinderhook after his hometown in New York, formed O.K. Clubs, which spread the letters across the country.

The origin was pinned down in the 1960s by Columbia University scholar Allen Walker Read, who debunked a long list of rival theories. It's a reminder that language often grows out of play, not planning, and that the strangest-looking words sometimes have the simplest stories.
cards.example: The same pattern continues today: LOL, OMG and BRB started as in-group shorthand before going mainstream. Next time you type OK, you're using a 187-year-old Boston joke.
cards.takeaway: OK started as oll korrect, a joke abbreviation that politics made permanent.

cards.title: Inversion: solve problems backwards
cards.body:
The mathematician Carl Jacobi advised "invert, always invert", and Charlie Munger made it famous as a thinking tool. Instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, and then avoid those things.

Inversion works because failure is often easier to see than success. It's hard to define the perfect investment process, but easy to list ways to blow up: excessive leverage, buying things you don't understand, selling in a panic. Remove those and you're already ahead of most people.

A close cousin is the pre-mortem, developed by psychologist Gary Klein. Before a project starts, the team imagines it has failed spectacularly and writes down why. This gives people permission to voice doubts they'd otherwise keep quiet, and surfaces risks while there's still time to address them.
cards.example: Planning to run a half marathon in the spring? Invert: how would you guarantee not finishing? Ramp mileage too fast, skimp on sleep, never practise fuelling, start too quickly. Your training plan is now mostly a list of those things to avoid.
cards.takeaway: To find the path to success, first map the ways to fail.

quiz.question: Why was October 31 called All Hallows' Eve?
options: It was the night of the harvest auction
It was the evening before All Saints' Day on November 1
It marked the first frost in Scotland
It honoured a saint named Hallow
quiz.explanation: November 1 was All Saints', or All Hallows', Day, so the night before was All Hallows' Eve, shortened to Halloween.

quiz.question: Company X has a $5B market cap, $3B of debt and $1B of cash. What is its enterprise value?
What makes Point Nemo notable?
options: It is the point in the ocean farthest from any land
It is the deepest point in the ocean
It is where the Pacific and Atlantic meet
It is the windiest place on Earth
quiz.explanation: Point Nemo is about 2,700 km from the nearest land in every direction, which is why spacecraft are crashed there.

quiz.question: What was unusual about the making of Rumours?
options: It was recorded live in a single take
It was the band's debut album
Band members were breaking up with each other while recording it
It was recorded without any guitars
quiz.explanation: Two couples in the band were splitting up, and they wrote and sang songs about each other.

quiz.question: How did OK spread beyond a Boston newspaper joke?
options: Telegraph operators adopted it as an official code
Supporters of Martin Van Buren, 'Old Kinderhook', formed O.K. Clubs in 1840
It came from a word used by soldiers in the War of 1812
It was printed on early bank notes
quiz.explanation: The 1840 election campaign gave the joke abbreviation a second meaning and spread it nationwide.

quiz.question: Which of these is an example of inversion?
options: Copying the habits of the most successful person you know
Setting a bigger goal to motivate yourself
Averaging several forecasts
Listing what would guarantee a project fails, then avoiding those things
quiz.explanation: Inversion flips the question from 'how do I succeed?' to 'what would make me fail?'
